section.title: Penalties for Sin
section.sectionRationale: This chapter supplies the civil penalties, largely capital, for many of the offenses named in chapters 18 and 19, Molech worship, occult practices, cursing parents, and specific sexual sins, functioning as Israel's old covenant enforcement of the holiness just described.
section.thesis: God attaches severe, largely capital civil penalties to Israel's most serious covenant violations, showing how seriously He regards both fidelity to Him and the purity of family life, while entrusting the actual execution of judgment to Israel's courts as a whole community, not to individuals.
section.frameNote: Three movements: capital penalties for Molech worship and consulting mediums; penalties for cursing parents and a list of sexual offenses paralleling chapter 18; and the closing call to be holy and set apart, since the LORD has set Israel apart from the nations.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Tell the Israelites, ‘Any Israelite or foreigner living in Israel who gives any of his children to Molech must be put to death. The people of the land are to stone him.
And I will set My face against that man and cut him off from his people, because by giving his offspring to Molech, he has defiled My sanctuary and {{chalal|profaned}} My holy name.
And if the people of the land ever hide their eyes and fail to put to death the man who gives one of his children to Molech,
then I will set My face against that man and his family and cut off from among their people both him and all who follow him in prostituting themselves with Molech.
Whoever turns to mediums or spiritists to prostitute himself with them, I will also set My face against that person and cut him off from his people.
Consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, because I am the LORD your God.
And you shall keep My statutes and practice them. I am the LORD who sanctifies you.
If anyone curses his father or mother, he must be put to death. He has cursed his father or mother; his {{dam|blood}} shall be upon him.
If a man commits adultery with another man’s wife, with the wife of his neighbor, both the adulterer and the adulteress must surely be put to death.
If a man lies with his father’s wife, he has uncovered his father’s nakedness. Both must surely be put to death; their blood is upon them.
If a man lies with his daughter-in-law, both must surely be put to death. They have acted perversely; their blood is upon them.
If a man lies with a man as with a woman, they have both committed an {{toevah|abomination}}. They must surely be put to death; their blood is upon them.
If a man marries both a woman and her mother, it is depraved. Both he and they must be burned in the fire, so that there will be no depravity among you.
If a man lies carnally with an animal, he must be put to death. And you are also to kill the animal.
If a woman approaches any animal to mate with it, you must kill both the woman and the animal. They must surely be put to death; their blood is upon them.

If a man marries his sister, whether the daughter of his father or of his mother, and they have sexual relations, it is a disgrace. They must be cut off in the sight of their people. He has uncovered the nakedness of his sister; he shall bear his iniquity.

If a man lies with a menstruating woman and has sexual relations with her, he has exposed the source of her flow, and she has uncovered the source of her blood. Both of them must be cut off from among their people.
You must not have sexual relations with the sister of your mother or your father, for it is exposing one’s own kin; both shall bear their iniquity.
If a man lies with his uncle’s wife, he has uncovered the nakedness of his uncle. They will bear their sin; they shall die childless.
If a man marries his brother’s wife, it is an act of impurity. He has uncovered the nakedness of his brother; they shall be childless.

units.label: Set apart, and holy to the LORD

verses.text: You are therefore to keep all My statutes and ordinances, so that the land where I am bringing you to live will not vomit you out.
You must not follow the statutes of the nations I am driving out before you. Because they did all these things, I abhorred them.

But I have told you that you will inherit their land, since I will give it to you as an inheritance, a land flowing with milk and honey. I am the LORD your God, who has set you apart from the peoples.

You are therefore to distinguish between clean and unclean animals and birds. Do not become contaminated by any animal or bird, or by anything that crawls on the ground; I have set these apart as unclean for you.
You are to be {{qadosh|holy}} to Me because I, the LORD, am holy, and I have set you apart from the nations to be My own.
A man or a woman who is a medium or spiritist must surely be put to death. They shall be stoned; their blood is upon them.’”

chalal.gloss: To profane, defile, or treat as common what should be holy. Applied here to giving a child to Molech, this word marks the offense as an assault not merely on the child but on God's own reputation and holy name.

dam.gloss: Blood. The recurring formula their blood is upon them or his blood is upon him places responsibility for a capital sentence squarely on the guilty party, rather than on the community that carries it out.

toevah.gloss: Abomination, something detestable. Applied here, as in chapter 18, to a specific sexual act, this word carries the same strong moral weight it carries elsewhere in the Old Testament for idolatry and dishonest business practice.

qadosh.gloss: Holy, set apart. The chapter closes as it began in chapter 19, grounding Israel's whole ethical and civil order in the character of the LORD Himself, who has set Israel apart from the nations to belong to Him.

basic.context: This chapter assigns civil penalties, mostly execution by the community, to the offenses named in chapters 18 and 19: child sacrifice to Molech, consulting mediums, cursing parents, adultery, incest, same sex relations, and bestiality.
basic.hermeneutics: This is Israel's old covenant civil and judicial law, tied to its unique status as a theocratic nation under God's direct rule in the land. The New Testament nowhere directs the church or civil governments to enforce these specific penalties; the church's own discipline for comparable sin is exclusion from fellowship aimed at repentance and restoration, not execution, 1 Corinthians 5:1-5, 13.
basic.originalLanguages: The recurring formula their blood is upon them places moral responsibility for the capital sentence on the guilty party rather than the community executing it. Chalal, profane, marks Molech worship as an assault on God's own name; toevah, abomination, applies the same strong term used in chapter 18 to specific sexual sin; qadosh, holy, closes the chapter as it opened the last, grounding everything in God's own character.
basic.typology: The chapter's repeated sentence of death for unrepented sin points toward the judgment Christ bore in His people's place; and Israel's status as a people set apart from the nations anticipates the church, a holy nation, God's own possession, set apart not by land or bloodline but by union with Christ.
basic.christ: Galatians 3:13 says Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us; the severity of this chapter's penalties shows exactly what judgment sin deserves, a judgment Christ bore in the place of all who trust Him, so that the sentence of death this chapter pronounces is, for believers, already fully borne by their substitute.
basic.god: God's holiness demands that covenant violations touching worship and family integrity be treated as matters of life and death for the whole community, not private preference; yet the reason given for holiness is God's own character, not mere fear of penalty, and in Christ deserved judgment gives way to mercy for all who repent.
basic.crossReferences: Galatians 3:13 says Christ became a curse for us to redeem us from the law's curse. 1 Corinthians 5:1-5, 13 shows the church's actual practice with serious sin among believers, exclusion and restoration, not execution. Hebrews 12:24 contrasts the blood that cries for judgment with the blood of Christ, which speaks a better word.
basic.oneStory: This chapter shows exactly how seriously God regards sin against Himself and against the family He designed; it prepares the way for the gospel's full weight, since Christ bore precisely the judgment this chapter pronounces, in the place of everyone who turns to Him, so that mercy, not merely punishment, becomes the last word.

context.literary:
Leviticus 20 is built as a frame around a list. The outer frame is holiness: verses 7 and 8 call Israel to 'consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy,' and verses 22 to 26 return to the same call, ending with the reason, 'I, the LORD, am holy, and I have set you apart from the nations to be My own.' Inside that frame sit the penalties, and the whole unit is bracketed by two capital laws about the spirit world, Molech and mediums at the start, verses 2 to 6, and mediums and spiritists again at the very end, verse 27. The chapter begins and ends with false worship, and the family laws sit in between.

The list itself is ordered by severity. Verses 9 to 16 carry the death penalty, marked by the repeated verdict 'their blood is upon them.' Verses 17 to 19 speak of being 'cut off' or bearing iniquity, and verses 20 and 21 end with childlessness. The writer moves from the courts' sentence down to sentences that God Himself carries out.

The relation to chapter 18 matters. Chapter 18 gave the same offenses in the form of direct prohibitions, 'You must not,' addressed to each Israelite. Chapter 20 recasts many of them as case law, 'If a man,' with the consequence attached. Chapter 18 speaks to the conscience; chapter 20 speaks to the community that must judge. Between them stands chapter 19, the positive portrait of holiness, so that chapters 18 to 20 form a single block: what not to do, what holiness looks like, and what happens when the line is crossed.

Finally, the chapter ties the moral laws to the food laws of chapter 11. The verb that says God has 'set you apart' in verses 24 and 26 is the same verb that tells Israel to 'distinguish' clean from unclean animals in verse 25. The separation at the table was meant to rehearse the separation of the whole life.
context.historical:
The laws are addressed to a people about to enter Canaan, and verse 23 names the reason for their sharpness: 'You must not follow the statutes of the nations I am driving out before you. Because they did all these things, I abhorred them.' The practices listed were not hypothetical. Later Israelite history records kings who 'sacrificed his son in the fire, according to the abominations of the nations,' 2 Kings 16:3, and places the rite at Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom outside Jerusalem, 2 Kings 23:10 and Jeremiah 32:35. The name of that valley, through its Greek form Gehenna, later became a word for final judgment.

Necromancy was also a live temptation. Saul had 'removed the mediums and spiritists from the land,' 1 Samuel 28:3, in obedience to laws like this one, yet on the eve of his death he went to a medium at Endor, and the Chronicler names that act among the reasons 'Saul died for his unfaithfulness to the LORD,' 1 Chronicles 10:13.

The procedure assumes a community with courts and witnesses. The 'people of the land,' verse 2, are the whole body of citizens, and the execution is public and corporate, most often by stoning outside the camp. Elsewhere the law requires more than one witness, Deuteronomy 17:6, and forbids punishing children for their fathers' crimes, Deuteronomy 24:16. Verse 4 anticipates a community that 'hide their eyes,' preferring not to act, which shows that even in Israel the penalties were resisted as well as enforced. Where the people failed, God warned that He would act Himself, verse 5.

The mention of land that 'will not vomit you out,' verse 22, picks up Leviticus 18:25-28. The land is pictured as a living thing that cannot stomach defilement. Israel's tenure in Canaan was conditional on the holiness these laws protected, and the exile would later prove the warning true.
context.canonical:
The chapter's influence runs through the rest of the Law and the Prophets. Deuteronomy repeats the ban on child sacrifice and on consulting the dead in one breath, Deuteronomy 18:10-12, and gives the same reason, that these practices are why the nations are being driven out. The historical books then measure kings by it: Ahaz and Manasseh fall, and Josiah's reform is praised because he desecrated Topheth, 2 Kings 23:10. Jeremiah calls the Molech rite 'something I never commanded them, nor had it ever entered My mind,' Jeremiah 32:35, a sharp rebuke to anyone who thought such offerings could please the LORD.

Jesus quotes verse 9 directly. When the Pharisees used their tradition to excuse neglect of parents, He answered, 'For God said, Honor your father and mother and Anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death,' Matthew 15:4, with the parallel at Mark 7:10. He did not treat the penalty as embarrassing; He used it to show how seriously God takes the fifth commandment. John the Baptist applied verse 21 to Herod, 'It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife,' Mark 6:18.

Paul reads the chapter through the cross and the church. In 1 Corinthians 5 a man living with his father's wife, the very case of verse 11, is to be removed from the fellowship, and Paul borrows Deuteronomy's formula, 'Expel the wicked man from among you,' 1 Corinthians 5:13. In 1 Corinthians 6:9-11 he lists many of the same sins, then adds, 'And that is what some of you were. But you were washed.' The call to separation in verses 24 to 26 is echoed in 2 Corinthians 6:17 and 7:1, and Peter applies 'Be holy, because I am holy' to believers, 1 Peter 1:16. Revelation 21:8 and 22:15 place sorcerers and the sexually immoral outside the city, showing that the moral line drawn here stands to the end.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wrote to make Israel feel the weight of two kinds of sin at once: sin against God's exclusive claim on worship, and sin against the order of the family He had made. By setting Molech and mediums at the edges of the list and the family laws in the middle, the chapter treats them as one reality. To give a child to another god and to break the boundaries of the household both tear at the covenant, because the family was the place where the knowledge of the LORD was to be passed on, Deuteronomy 6:6-7.

He also meant the community to own its responsibility. Verse 4 addresses those who 'hide their eyes,' and verse 5 warns that God will act against the offender and 'his family' and 'all who follow him.' The people could not treat these sins as private matters between consenting adults or as a family's own business. Tolerated defilement would spread.

Above all, Moses wanted Israel to understand the motive of holiness. The penalties are not the point of the chapter; the frame is. Israel was to keep these statutes because 'I am the LORD who sanctifies you,' verse 8, and because God had already set them apart as His own, verse 26. The law follows grace: separation is not how Israel became God's people, it is how God's people were to live.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is prescriptive for Israel as a nation under covenant in the land. Its penalties were real commands for Israel's courts. That does not make them commands for every nation or for the church, because the setting that gave them force, a theocracy in which civil and religious community were one, has not been carried forward. The New Testament never hands the sword of these laws to the church; Paul's instruction in 1 Corinthians 5 is exclusion, and his aim is that the offender's spirit 'may be saved on the Day of the Lord,' 1 Corinthians 5:5.

What does carry forward is the moral evaluation beneath the penalties. The New Testament reaffirms the wrongness of idolatry, sorcery, adultery, incest and the other sexual sins listed here, Galatians 5:19-21 and 1 Corinthians 6:9-10. The chapter therefore teaches Christians what God thinks of these acts, not what the state must do with them. It also teaches the church not to 'hide its eyes' when serious sin is present, and to hold together seriousness about sin and hope of restoration, as 2 Corinthians 2:6-8 does.

debates.question: Do the capital penalties in this chapter apply to civil law or church practice today?

views.label: Tied to Israel's theocracy and fulfilled in Christ
views.case: Israel was a unique covenant nation under God's direct rule, with its own land and civil structure. The New Testament nowhere directs the church or civil governments to enforce these specific penalties, and the church's discipline for comparable sin is exclusion from fellowship aimed at repentance, not execution, 1 Corinthians 5:1-5, 13. The Westminster Confession states the classic Reformed version: the judicial laws expired with the state of that people, binding others only so far as their general equity requires.

views.label: The penalties still express the ideal standard for civil justice
views.case: A minority, usually called theonomists, argue that because God gave these penalties, they reveal what just punishment is, and that Christian societies should move toward them. They appeal to Jesus' words that not a stroke of the Law will pass away, Matthew 5:17-18, and to His use of verse 9 in Matthew 15:4.

views.label: A witness to the seriousness of these sins even where the penalty does not transfer
views.case: Many who agree the death penalty itself does not carry over recognise that the severity here shows how gravely God regards these acts. That severity should inform, without dictating, how the church teaches, disciplines and cares pastorally, and it should keep Christians from treating any of these sins lightly.

debates.bearing: The first and third views together fit the New Testament best. Christians live under civil governments, not the Mosaic theocracy, and the apostles redirect serious sin among believers toward discipline aimed at repentance. The moral verdict remains, and so does the grace that met it at the cross.

debates.question: What does being 'cut off' mean, and who does the cutting?

views.label: A form of execution or banishment carried out by the community
views.case: Some read 'cut off from his people' as a judicial penalty, either death or expulsion from the covenant community, parallel to the stoning commanded in verse 2. Exodus 31:14 places 'put to death' and 'cut off' side by side for the same offense.

views.label: A penalty God Himself executes
views.case: Others note that in verses 3, 5 and 6 God says 'I will set My face against' the offender and 'cut him off,' in the first person. On this view the penalty is divine: early death, the ending of a family line, or exclusion from the people's future, left in God's hands where human courts cannot or do not act. The childlessness of verses 20 and 21 supports this.

debates.bearing: The chapter itself distinguishes the two. Where the court is to act, it says so; where God acts, He says 'I will.' Verses 4 and 5 show the second stepping in when the first fails. The penalty was not only a human sentence but the withdrawal of God's favour, which is why Numbers 15:31 adds that 'his guilt remains on him.'

debates.question: Does 'burned in the fire' in verse 14 mean burning alive?

views.label: Execution by fire
views.case: The plain wording names fire as the means, as in Judah's sentence on Tamar, 'Let her be burned to death,' Genesis 38:24, and the same penalty for the priest's daughter in Leviticus 21:9.

views.label: Burning after execution
views.case: Others point to Joshua 7:25, where Achan and his household are first stoned and their bodies then burned. Burning would then be an added mark of disgrace on the dead rather than the means of death. Later Jewish tradition developed its own, different interpretation of the method.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle the procedure, and certainty is not possible. What is clear is the purpose it states: 'so that there will be no depravity among you.' The sentence aimed at removing a corruption from the community, which is the concern Paul carries into the church in 1 Corinthians 5:6-7.

study.originalLanguages:
The name Molech has the same consonants as melek, king, and many scholars think the vowels were deliberately altered in Hebrew tradition to recall a word for shame. That point is widely held but not certain. What the text itself makes plain in verse 5 is that Israel's allegiance was at stake: to go 'prostituting themselves with Molech' uses zanah, the verb of sexual unfaithfulness, for worship given to another god, as Judges 2:17 does. The same verb is used for turning to mediums in verse 6. Idolatry is pictured as adultery against the LORD.

The mediums and spiritists of verses 6 and 27 are ovot and yiddonim. The second word is usually connected with the root yada, to know, suggesting 'knowing ones' who claimed access to hidden knowledge from the dead. Deuteronomy 18:11 sets the same pair beside anyone who 'inquires of the dead.' The law forbids the attempt to know what God has not revealed by going around Him.

In verse 9 the verb 'curses' is qalal, whose basic sense is to be light, to treat as trivial. The BSB footnote gives 'dishonors or reviles.' It is the exact opposite of the verb in the fifth commandment, kabed, 'honor,' whose root sense is to be heavy, Exodus 20:12. To curse a parent is to make light of those God commanded Israel to treat as weighty.

The verdicts use a cluster of strong words. Verse 12 calls a man's relations with his daughter-in-law tebel, 'perversely,' the word used for bestiality in Leviticus 18:23; it suggests confusion, a mixing of what God kept distinct. Verse 14 calls marriage to a woman and her mother zimmah, 'depraved,' as Leviticus 18:17 does. Verse 17 calls marriage to a sister chesed, 'a disgrace.' This is a different word from the chesed that means covenant love; it is a rare homonym meaning shame, and Proverbs 14:34 uses it in 'sin is a disgrace to any people.' Verse 21 calls taking a brother's wife niddah, 'impurity,' the word used for menstrual uncleanness, so that the act is described as ritually polluting as well as morally wrong.

The refrain 'their blood is upon them,' demehem bam, is a legal formula of responsibility. It appears in other forms in Joshua 2:19 and Ezekiel 18:13, 'his blood will be on his own head.' The one who dies under this sentence has brought it on himself, so the community that carries it out does not incur bloodguilt.

Finally, the verb badal, to separate or distinguish, ties the chapter's close together. God has 'set you apart from the peoples,' verse 24; Israel must 'distinguish between clean and unclean,' verse 25; God has 'set you apart from the nations,' verse 26. It is the verb of Genesis 1:4, where God 'separated the light from the darkness.' Israel's holiness is a small reenactment of creation's ordering.

typology.type: The repeated verdict 'their blood is upon them,' marking personal responsibility for capital guilt
typology.fulfillment: The formula places the guilt of a death on the one who deserved it. The gospel turns this upside down. At the trial of Jesus the crowd cried, 'His blood be on us and on our children!' Matthew 27:25, yet His blood is the one blood that does not condemn but cleanses. Hebrews 12:24 says it 'speaks a better word than the blood of Abel,' blood that cried out from the ground for justice, Genesis 4:10. The type falls short because the guilty in Leviticus bore their own blood; in Christ the Innocent bears the blood of the guilty, Romans 3:25-26.

typology.type: Israel set apart from the nations as holy, verse 26
typology.fulfillment: God separated Israel from the peoples by land, law and table, and warned them not to follow the nations' statutes. The church inherits the identity: 'a holy nation, a people for God's own possession,' 1 Peter 2:9-10. The escalation is that the separation is no longer drawn by territory or ethnicity; it is drawn by union with Christ, and it now gathers people from the very nations Israel was separated from. Paul applies the call 'come out from among them and be separate' to the church in 2 Corinthians 6:17, where the separation is from idols and defilement, not from Gentile neighbours.

typology.type: Distinguishing clean from unclean animals, verse 25
typology.fulfillment: The food laws were a daily sign that God had set Israel apart, a lesson rehearsed at every meal. When the gospel went to the Gentiles, God took up that very sign to announce the change: Peter's vision of unclean animals ended with, 'Do not call anything impure that God has made clean,' Acts 10:15, and Peter understood it of people, Acts 10:28. The type falls short and is set aside once its reality arrives. The distinction that separated Jew and Gentile is fulfilled in a people cleansed by faith, while the moral holiness it pictured remains, 2 Corinthians 7:1.

typology.type: The land that vomits out its defiled inhabitants, verse 22
typology.fulfillment: Canaan could not hold a people who practised these things; the nations were expelled, and Israel was warned that it would be too. Scripture carries the picture forward to the final inheritance. The new creation is a home 'where righteousness dwells,' 2 Peter 3:13, and 'nothing unclean will ever enter it,' Revelation 21:27. The difference is that Israel could only be warned; those who inherit the new earth do so because they have been washed, 1 Corinthians 6:11, and made fit for a land that will never cast them out.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by the sentence it pronounces. Almost every verse ends in death or being cut off, and the reader is left with the question the Law cannot answer: what becomes of those who have done these things? Paul answers directly. 'All who rely on works of the law are under a curse,' Galatians 3:10, and 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13, quoting Deuteronomy 21:23 about the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree. The penalty of the Law's worst cases was the form of death Jesus accepted. He was executed outside the city, Hebrews 13:12, as the condemned in Israel were taken outside the camp.

It leads to Christ by the holiness it demands. Verse 8 says, 'I am the LORD who sanctifies you.' Israel could not make itself holy, and the chapter's own frame admits it. In Christ that promise is kept at its root: 'For them I sanctify Myself, so that they too may be sanctified by the truth,' John 17:19. Believers are 'washed, sanctified, justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 6:11, and Paul says that immediately after naming many of the very sins listed here.

It leads to Christ by the family it protects. The chapter defends the honour of father and mother and the integrity of marriage. Jesus upheld verse 9 against those who evaded it, Matthew 15:4, and He deepened the law of adultery to the heart, Matthew 5:27-28, which places every reader under its verdict. The church He founds is a household where the broken can be received and made new.

It leads to Christ by contrast with Molech. The Canaanite rite gave children to a god in the fire to secure blessing. The gospel reverses it completely: God does not demand our children; He gives His own Son. 'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The Father who condemned the sacrifice of sons in verse 2 is the Father who Himself gave the Son, not to buy favour from a hostile power, but to bring rebels home.

A word of care keeps the reading honest. The chapter is not a coded picture of Jesus. Its links to Christ run through the New Testament's own use of the curse, the call to holiness and the command to honour parents, and through the plain problem it leaves unresolved, which only a Substitute can meet.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is that He will not share His worship. Molech worship is said to have 'defiled My sanctuary and profaned My holy name,' verse 3. The offense is not only against the child but against God's reputation, because Israel bore His name among the nations. The same God who would later say 'I will not yield My glory to another,' Isaiah 42:8, here guards His name with the severest sanction the law knows.

He is personally engaged in justice. Three times in verses 3 to 6 He says, 'I will set My face against,' the same expression used for His judgment in Leviticus 17:10 and 26:17. God's face turned toward His people is the blessing of Numbers 6:25; His face set against a person is its terrible reverse. And when the community fails to act, verse 4, God does not shrug. Justice does not depend finally on human courts.

He is the Creator who orders and separates. The verb that tells us God 'set you apart,' verses 24 and 26, is the verb of creation's first day, Genesis 1:4. The sexual laws in the centre of the chapter protect distinctions God built into human life: between generations, between kin, between human and animal. To blur them is called 'perversely' and 'depraved,' because it undoes something God made.

He is the God who gives before He demands. Verse 24 speaks of an inheritance, 'a land flowing with milk and honey,' and of a people already set apart. The call to holiness in verse 26 rests on two facts about God: 'I, the LORD, am holy,' and 'I have set you apart... to be My own.' Holiness is not a price for belonging; it is the shape belonging takes.

The chapter holds together a tension the whole Bible lives with. God abhors the practices of the nations, verse 23, yet He will later call those same nations to Himself, Isaiah 56:6-7. His holiness is not ethnic preference but moral purity, and His severity toward sin is the measure of His commitment to the good of those He made.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to fear the Lord rightly, to refuse every rival loyalty, and to see in the gravity of these penalties the size of the mercy shown at the cross, where God is revealed as 'just and... the one who justifies,' Romans 3:26.

crossReferences.note: The companion chapter gives the same offenses as prohibitions and explains why they matter: the land itself is defiled and 'will vomit out its inhabitants.' Leviticus 20:22 repeats the image. Chapter 18 speaks to each Israelite's conscience; chapter 20 attaches the consequences for the community.

Moses repeats the ban on child sacrifice and on mediums and spiritists together, as Leviticus 20:2-6 does, and names them the reason the LORD is driving out the nations. The pairing shows that giving children to a god and consulting the dead were seen as two faces of the same rebellion.

Josiah 'desecrated Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech.' This is the practice Leviticus 20:2-5 condemns, carried on in Judah for generations, and ended by a king who finally enforced the law.

The Chronicler says Saul died for his unfaithfulness, in part because he 'consulted a medium for guidance.' Saul had himself removed the mediums, 1 Samuel 28:3, in line with Leviticus 20:6 and 27, and then turned to one. The verse shows the law's warning working out in Israel's first king.

Jesus quotes Leviticus 20:9 alongside the fifth commandment to expose tradition that let people evade care for their parents. He treats the capital penalty as a measure of how seriously God takes honour to father and mother, not as an embarrassment to be explained away.

John the Baptist tells Herod, 'It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife.' Herod had married Herodias, his brother's wife, the case named in Leviticus 20:21. John applied the Levitical law to a ruler, and it cost him his life.

A man in Corinth has his father's wife, the offense of Leviticus 20:11. Paul calls for his removal from the church, echoing Deuteronomy's 'Expel the wicked man from among you.' The penalty is exclusion, not death, and its goal is that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord.

Paul lists idolaters, adulterers and those who practise homosexual acts among those who will not inherit the kingdom, many of the sins of Leviticus 20. Then he adds, 'And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified.' The verdict stands, and so does the rescue.

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, citing the law about a hanged criminal. The death sentences of Leviticus 20 express that curse in its sharpest form, and Paul says Jesus took the curse itself upon Himself on behalf of all who believe.

Believers have come to 'the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.' Abel's blood cried out for justice. In Leviticus 20 the guilty bear their own blood. Christ's blood speaks for pardon, answering the verdict the chapter keeps repeating.

Paul gathers Levitical promises, 'I will dwell with them and walk among them,' and the call to 'be separate' and 'touch no unclean thing.' He concludes that believers should cleanse themselves from everything that defiles, perfecting holiness in the fear of God, carrying Leviticus 20:24-26 into the church.

Peter calls the church 'a holy nation, a people for God's own possession,' language drawn from Israel's calling. Leviticus 20:26 says God set Israel apart 'to be My own.' The church now bears that identity, set apart not by territory but by the mercy of God in Christ.

study.oneStory:
Leviticus 20 answers a question raised in Genesis. When the first family broke, the fracture ran straight into the next generation: Cain killed his brother, and by Genesis 6 the earth was filled with violence. The world outside Eden is a world where families are damaged and worship goes astray. The nations of Canaan are presented here as that story's far end, peoples whose statutes had become so corrupt that God 'abhorred them,' verse 23, and the land could no longer hold them.

Into that world God set one people apart. Israel was meant to be a picture of restored humanity: a people whose worship belonged to one God, whose families kept the boundaries He made, and whose table rehearsed daily that they belonged to Him. The laws of this chapter guarded that picture with the gravest penalties because the picture carried the promise to Abraham that the nations would be blessed through his offspring. If Israel became like Canaan, the light would go out.

Israel did become like Canaan. The Molech rite was practised in Jerusalem itself, Jeremiah 32:35, and mediums were consulted by kings. The land did what verse 22 warned and cast its people out into exile. The chapter's sentence fell on the nation as a whole, and the prophets saw that only a new heart could keep a law like this, Ezekiel 36:26-27.

The story turns in Christ. He bore the curse the chapter pronounces, Galatians 3:13, and gathered a new people from Jew and Gentile alike, washed and sanctified, 1 Corinthians 6:11. That people is still called to be holy, 1 Peter 1:15-16, and to deal with serious sin in its midst, but with a discipline that aims at restoration because the death penalty has been paid.

The story ends where verse 22 pointed. There will be an inheritance that does not vomit out its people, a new earth where righteousness dwells. Outside are the sorcerers and the sexually immoral who refused to be washed, Revelation 22:15. Inside, God dwells with a people He has fully set apart, and the holiness this chapter demanded will be simply what they are.

quiz.q: What penalty is prescribed for giving one's child to Molech?

options.text: Death by stoning at the hands of the community.
options.note: Verse 2 specifies this penalty explicitly.

options.text: A fine paid to the priest.
options.note: The text specifies execution, not a monetary fine.

options.text: Temporary exile from the camp.
options.note: Verse 2 specifies death, not temporary exile.

options.text: No penalty is specified.
options.note: Verse 2 explicitly specifies the penalty of death by stoning.

quiz.q: What happens if the community fails to execute the penalty against someone who gives a child to Molech, according to verses 4-5?

options.text: God Himself will set His face against that man and his family and cut them off from among their people.
options.note: Verses 4-5 state this consequence directly.

options.text: The matter is simply forgotten.
options.note: Verses 4-5 explicitly describe God's own judgment in that case.

options.text: The community itself is rewarded for leniency.
options.note: The text describes divine judgment, not reward, for failing to enforce this law.

options.text: No consequence is described.
options.note: Verses 4-5 explicitly describe a consequence.

quiz.q: What recurring phrase closes many of the individual case laws about sexual offenses in this chapter?

options.text: "Their blood is upon them," or "his blood shall be upon him."
options.note: This phrase recurs at verses 9, 11, 12, 13, 16, and 27.

options.text: "They shall be forgiven immediately."
options.note: The recurring phrase places responsibility for guilt on the offender, not immediate forgiveness.

options.text: "No punishment applies to this case."
options.note: The recurring phrase marks these as capital offenses, not cases without punishment.

options.text: No recurring phrase appears in the chapter.
options.note: The phrase recurs multiple times through the chapter.

quiz.q: What reason does God give in verses 22-26 for keeping all these statutes?

options.text: So the land will not vomit Israel out, since God has set them apart from the nations to be holy to Him.
options.note: Verses 22-26 state this reasoning directly, echoing chapter 18's warning.

options.text: So that Israel could gain military alliances with neighboring nations.
options.note: The stated reason concerns holiness and the land, not foreign alliances.

options.text: No reason is given for keeping these statutes.
options.note: Verses 22-26 give this reasoning explicitly.

options.text: So that Israel would become identical to the surrounding nations.
options.note: The text explicitly calls Israel to be different from, not identical to, the surrounding nations.

quiz.q: How does Galatians 3:13 relate to the severity of judgment described in this chapter?

options.text: It says Christ redeemed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse for us, bearing the judgment sin deserves.
options.note: Galatians 3:13 states this directly.

options.text: It says the law's curse no longer has any meaning or seriousness at all.
options.note: Galatians 3:13 takes the curse seriously enough that Christ must bear it Himself, rather than dismissing its seriousness.

options.text: It has no connection to this chapter's themes.
options.note: Galatians 3:13 speaks directly to the curse and judgment this chapter's penalties describe.

options.text: It teaches that believers must still bear this judgment themselves.
options.note: Galatians 3:13 teaches the opposite: Christ bore the curse in believers' place.

questions: This chapter shows how seriously God regards sin against Himself and against the family He designed. Where have you grown casual about sin that God actually takes with this much weight?

The repeated phrase 'their blood is upon them' places responsibility for judgment on the guilty party. How does it change your view of the cross to realize Christ took that very judgment upon Himself in your place?
Israel was called to be set apart, holy, different from the nations around them. In what specific area of your life is God calling you to a costly distinctiveness right now?

The New Testament church responds to serious sin among believers not with execution but with loving discipline aimed at repentance and restoration. Is there someone in your life who needs that kind of firm, hopeful correction from you?

This chapter's severity can be hard to read. Where do you need to bring your discomfort honestly to God in prayer, rather than either dismissing the text or losing sight of the mercy that follows it in Christ?

translationNotes.note: The people of the land are to stone him indicates community, not individual, execution of this penalty, reflecting the corporate nature of covenant responsibility in Israel's judicial system.

Burned in the fire likely describes the method of execution itself, or possibly the burning of the body after execution by another means, a point ancient interpreters debated; either way it marks the offense as especially severe.
They shall die childless may describe a divinely imposed consequence rather than an additional human penalty, distinguishing this case from those explicitly assigned execution.
